area: Area IX. Performance and Ground Reference Maneuvers
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain the aerodynamics, sensations and control forces of a steep turn, demonstrate a coordinated 360° steep turn at about 50° of bank each way from the right seat while explaining it (altitude ±100 feet, airspeed ±10 knots, bank ±5°, rollout ±10°), and spot, explain and fix the errors your learners will make.
why: The steep turn builds smooth, coordinated control, orientation to outside references, division of attention and a constant traffic scan [[24:210|AFH 10-1]]. It also lets a learner feel, at a safe altitude, how load factor and stall speed climb in a steep bank, the same trap behind stalls from steep turns near the ground [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]. As the instructor you have to fly it well while talking, watch someone else fly it, and know which error you are looking at and how to fix it.

prereading.what: Steep turns: purpose, forces, entry speed, procedure, trim, the nose-low recovery, the rollout lead and the 13 common errors. Read this twice.
prereading.label: AFH 10-1 to 10-3

prereading.what: Shallow, medium and steep turns; lift components; adverse yaw; slip and skid; turn radius; overbanking; posture and parallax.
prereading.label: AFH 3-12 to 3-16

prereading.what: Load factor, limit load factors, stall speed and load factor, VA and its limits, and judging load factor by seat pressure.
prereading.label: PHAK 5-33 to 5-37

prereading.what: Rate of turn and radius of turn formulas, worked examples and the canyon turn.
prereading.label: PHAK 5-38 to 5-41

prereading.what: Accelerated stalls, VA and VO with weight, and the cross-control stall.
prereading.label: AFH 5-19 to 5-20

prereading.what: Demonstration-performance, telling-and-doing, positive exchange of flight controls, distractions, integrated instruction, see and avoid, and correcting learner errors.
prereading.label: AIH 9-5 to 9-12

prereading.what: Instructional risk management: crowded practice areas, teaching at the wrong time or altitude, and getting the learner to call hazards.
prereading.label: AIH 10-7 to 10-8

warmup: Think first: your learner rolls into a steep turn, the nose sinks, and the altimeter starts to unwind. You can see it happen, but the learner pulls hard on the yoke and the bank gets steeper. Why does pulling make it worse, how would you have caught it 5 seconds earlier, and what would you say so the learner fixes it next time without you?

key_terms.def: One or more 360° or 720° turns, in one or both directions, at a bank between 45° and 60° [[24:210|AFH 10-1]].
The ratio of the total load on the airplane to its weight, in Gs. In a level turn it depends only on bank: 1.41 at 45° and 2.0 at 60° [[1:130|PHAK 5-33]] [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].
Any stall at more than +1 G, as in a turn or pull-up, so it comes at a higher indicated airspeed than the 1 G stall [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

The highest speed at which the design limit load can be imposed by gusts or full one-sided deflection of one control without structural damage. It goes down as weight goes down [[24:124|AFH 5-19]] [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].
In a steep bank the outside wing flies faster and makes more lift, so the bank keeps steepening unless opposite aileron is held [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].
Rudder used with aileron to cancel adverse yaw, so the pilot feels pressed straight down into the seat [[24:73|AFH 3-12]] [[24:74|AFH 3-13]].
Because the pilot sits to one side of the roll axis, the nose seems to rise in turns toward that side and drop in turns away from it [[24:76|AFH 3-15]].
Four phases: explanation, demonstration, learner performance with instructor supervision, and evaluation [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].
Instructor tells and does, learner tells while instructor does, learner tells and does, then learner does while the instructor evaluates [[25:177|AIH 9-7]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
A three-step spoken handover ('You have the flight controls', 'I have the flight controls', 'You have the flight controls') with a visual check [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
Absorption in one task to the exclusion of others, such as staring at one instrument while other parts of the performance slip [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

The principle that what is learned first often creates a strong, almost unshakable impression, so the instructor teaches it correctly and makes sure the learner gets it right the first time [[25:64|AIH 3-13]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

chunks.title: Purpose, procedure and the CFI standard

body.p: A steep turn is one or more level 360° or 720° turns, in one or both directions, at a bank between 45° and 60°. Its purpose is to build smooth, coordinated control, awareness of the airplane's orientation to outside references, division of attention, and a constant scan for traffic and hazards [[24:210|AFH 10-1]].

The procedure in one breath: clear the area, pick a distant reference for the rollout, set the manufacturer's entry speed, VA or VO, roll smoothly to the chosen bank, and generally before 30° add back pressure and power. Hold the bank, altitude and speed, then start the rollout about half the bank angle before the entry heading while easing off back pressure, trim and power [[24:211|AFH 10-2]] [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].

head: What the examiner sees
CFI ACS standard
rows: The manufacturer's recommended airspeed; or if one is not available, an airspeed not to exceed maneuvering speed (VA) (ACS AI.IX.A.S2)
A coordinated 360° steep turn with approximately a 50° bank (ACS AI.IX.A.S3)
Perform the Task in the opposite direction (ACS AI.IX.A.S4)
Entry altitude ±100 feet, airspeed ±10 knots, bank ±5°, roll out on the entry heading ±10° (ACS AI.IX.A.S5)
Analyze and correct common errors related to this Task (ACS AI.IX.A.S6)

body.p: Two things are new on the CFI test. First, you demonstrate and explain at the same time: the ACS skills line reads 'demonstrates and simultaneously explains.' Second, S6 asks you to analyze and correct errors, so expect the examiner to fly a flawed turn as your learner. Your learners' standards differ: the private ACS asks for approximately 45° and the opposite direction only as specified by the evaluator (ACS PA.V.A.S3, S4); the commercial ACS asks for approximately 50° both ways, the same as yours (ACS CA.V.A.S3, S4).

callout.text: For an ASEL CFI test, the evaluator must pick at least four Area IX Tasks, including Task A (Steep Turns) or Task B (Steep Spiral) (ACS Area IX note). Prepare both.

check.q: What bank does the CFI ACS ask for, and how is that different from what a private learner flies?
check.a: Approximately 50° (ACS AI.IX.A.S3); the private ACS asks for approximately 45° (ACS PA.V.A.S3). Both use ±5° of bank.

body.p: In a bank, total lift tilts and splits into a vertical part that holds the airplane up and a horizontal part that turns it. The horizontal part, not the rudder, turns the airplane. To stay level you raise the angle of attack with back pressure and add power for the extra drag [[24:73|AFH 3-12]] [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

Maintaining coordinated flight: when you roll with aileron, the rising wing gets more lift and more drag, so the nose yaws away from the turn (adverse yaw). Rudder in the direction of the turn, applied with the aileron, cancels it. That is the rudder's job in a turn: to coordinate it [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]. The AFH also asks you to keep left-turning tendencies such as P-factor in mind, which take effective rudder and aileron coordination in a steep turn [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

Overbanking tendencies: the AFH sorts turns by how the airplane behaves. Shallow (about 20° or less): stability slowly levels the wings, so you hold some aileron into the turn. Medium (about 20° to 45°): the bank stays put with neutral aileron. Steep (about 45° or more): the airplane keeps rolling unless you hold opposite aileron [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

bullets: Why it happens: the outside wing travels a longer path in the same time, so it flies faster and makes more lift [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].
The cure: opposite aileron once the bank you want is reached; the amount depends on bank and airspeed [[24:73|AFH 3-12]] [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].
Side effect: the outside wing's extra lift also brings extra drag, which causes a slight slip that you correct with rudder [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].
Steep banks need opposite aileron and rudder to keep the bank from steepening [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

callout.text: Teaching line (application): 'At 50° the airplane wants to roll in further. Your job is to hold it there with a little top aileron, keep the back pressure in, and keep the ball centered with whatever rudder it takes.'
Holding uncoordinated control deflections can set up a spin, and that is most dangerous at low altitude such as the traffic pattern [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

check.q: Your learner says the rudder is what turns the airplane. How do you correct that?
check.a: The horizontal component of lift turns the airplane; the rudder only coordinates the turn by countering adverse yaw [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

body.p: Load factor and accelerated stalls: in a level, coordinated turn, every airplane at every airspeed gets the same load factor for a given bank. It is 1.41 at 45° and 2.0 at 60°, so at 60° the effective weight of the airplane and everyone in it doubles. A level turn at 75° exceeds the 3.8 G a standard category general aviation airplane is designed for [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

head: Bank in a level turn
Load factor
Stall speed vs. 1 G
rows: About 1.19 times (application of the square-root rule)
About 1.41 times; the AFH example goes from 50 to 70 knots [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]

body.p: The load factor rises at a terrific rate after about 45° or 50° [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor, so as bank increases in level flight the margin between stall speed and maneuvering speed shrinks [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. A stall at more than +1 G is an accelerated maneuver stall, and it is typically demonstrated during steep turns [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

bullets: Load factors matter for two reasons: you can overload the structure, and a higher load factor raises the stall speed so the airplane stalls at a speed that looks safe [[1:130|PHAK 5-33]].
Accelerated stalls are flown at about 45° of bank, never faster than the manufacturer's speed, VA or VO, and never with flaps extended [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
If the turn is coordinated at the stall, the nose pitches away from the pilot as in a wings-level stall; if not, the bank may change until the angle of attack is reduced [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Recovery: forward elevator to reduce the angle of attack and stop the stall warning, level the wings with aileron, coordinate with rudder, adjust power [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Stalls from abrupt maneuvers tend to be more aggressive and can surprise an inexperienced pilot; failure to recover at once may lead to a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

callout.text: A sudden, unexpected loss of control, particularly in a steep turn or from an abrupt pull near the ground, has caused many accidents [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].

check.q: Why is an accelerated stall 'typically demonstrated during steep turns'?
check.a: A steep turn already puts more than 1 G on the wing, so a little more back pressure produces a stall at a higher airspeed than the 1 G stall [[24:124|AFH 5-19]] [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

body.p: Maneuvering speed, including the impact of weight changes: because load factors are high, steep turns are flown at an airspeed not above VA or VO [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. At or below VA or VO the airplane reaches the critical angle of attack and stalls, unloading the wing, before it exceeds the design load limit. Above them, it can reach the limit load before the wing stalls, so more load can overstress it [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

Weight changes VA. It goes down as weight goes down: the FAA example is 100 knots heavily loaded but only 90 knots with a light load [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]] [[24:389|AFH G-17]]. The AFH tells pilots to know how VA or VO changes with weight [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. Application: a dual training flight with half fuel is often well under maximum weight, so the max-gross VA can be too fast.

bullets: VA must be in the AFM/POH of recently designed airplanes; for older airplanes the PHAK gives a rough estimate of 1.7 times the normal stall speed [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].
Stalling at a higher speed puts on a load factor equal to the square of the speed increase: 1.7 x 1.7 = 2.89 G [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].

VA protects for one full control input, one time, in one axis, in smooth air. It does not protect against several full inputs in one axis or full inputs in more than one axis at once [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].
Rapid, large alternating inputs can cause structural failure at any speed, even below VA [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

callout.text: Teaching move (application): have the learner look up the POH entry speed or VA for today's weight during the ground briefing and say it out loud before takeoff. It turns S2 into a planning habit instead of a number on a card.

check.q: Your student plans to use the max-gross VA for steep turns on a light airplane. Is that safe?
check.a: No. VA goes down as weight goes down, so the max-gross figure is too fast for a light airplane; use the POH steep turn speed or VA for the actual weight [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]] [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

body.p: Rate and radius of turn: at a given true airspeed, more bank gives a faster rate and a smaller circle. At a given bank, more airspeed gives a slower rate and a bigger circle [[24:75|AFH 3-14]]. Maximum turning performance for a given speed comes with a high bank, limited by structure, aerodynamics and power [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

bullets: Rate of turn (degrees per second) = 1,091 x tangent of bank / true airspeed in knots [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]] [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]].
Radius of turn (feet) = true airspeed squared / (11.26 x tangent of bank) [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]].
All airspeeds in these formulas are true airspeed [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]].
Double the speed at the same bank and the radius is four times as large [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]].

body.p: Worked numbers (application of the PHAK formulas): at 95 knots TAS and 50° of bank, rate = 1,091 x 1.192 / 95 = 13.7° per second, so a full 360° takes about 26 seconds, and the radius is 9,025 / (11.26 x 1.192) = about 673 feet. Tell your learner before the flight: the turn is short, so the rollout cue comes up fast.

The canyon example shows why this matters outside the practice area: at 30° of bank, an airplane at 120 knots needs about 4,000 feet to reverse course and gets out of a 5,000-foot canyon; one at 140 knots needs over 6,000 feet and does not. Airspeed is the most influential factor, and many pilots steepen the bank when slowing down would have been better [[1:138|PHAK 5-41]].

callout.text: Bank tightens the turn; speed widens it, and speed counts squared.

check.q: At the same bank, what does a 10 percent slower true airspeed do to the radius?
check.a: It shrinks it to about 81 percent, because radius goes with the square of true airspeed (0.9 x 0.9 = 0.81) [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]].

body.p: A first steep turn surprises people. The AFH lists what the pilot meets: higher G-forces, the overbanking tendency, a big loss of vertical lift, substantial pitch control pressures, and the need for more power to hold altitude at a constant airspeed [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

bullets: G-force: at 2 G the effective weight of everyone aboard doubles, and pilots may have trouble with orientation and movement when they first feel it [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

Pitch force: once at the bank, considerable force on the elevator is needed to stay level. Nose-up trim and power can take away some or all of it; certification standards do not set trim requirements [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].
Yaw feels strange: a large share of the yaw is felt as motion toward and away from the earth's surface, which can be confusing at first [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].
Seat pressure: load factor can be judged by feel of seat pressure, but control pressure is not a reliable index of load factor across different airplanes [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]] [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

Body sense can lie: the body cannot tell gravity from the accelerations of maneuvering; in VMC the eyes usually win [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]]. A skid, a slip and an uncoordinated turn can all feel like the same sideways push [[1:430|PHAK 17-8]].

body.p: The sight picture is part of the feel. The flat top of the cowling against the horizon gives the first bank reference; then cross-check the attitude indicator [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]. From the left seat the nose seems to rise in a left turn and drop in a right turn because of parallax: the pilot sits off the roll axis and moves lower in a left turn and higher in a right turn [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]. Application (the AFH describes only the left seat): from the right seat the same geometry works the other way, so in a right turn you move lower and the nose seems to rise. Check your own picture before you demonstrate from that seat.

callout.text: Brief the sensations before the flight. The AIH says to introduce anxiety-provoking maneuvers with care, explaining the aerodynamics, the physical sensations to expect and the recovery first, and to treat fears as normal [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

Watch for leaning away from the turn to stay upright; it spoils the visual references and should be corrected at once [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]. Rough air and abrupt maneuvers raise the odds of airsickness, and a flight should end as soon as incipient airsickness appears [[25:46|AIH 2-13]].

check.q: Why is 'it feels like a lot of back pressure' a poor guide to load factor in a new airplane?
check.a: Control leverage differs between airplanes, so control pressure is not an index of load factor; seat pressure is the better feel cue [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]] [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

body.p: Build the lesson on solid fundamentals. Performance maneuvers should not be taught until the pilot shows consistent competency in the basics; start with a detailed ground lesson for each maneuver, and use segmented building blocks with enough repetition [[24:210|AFH 10-1]]. New learning rests on a foundation of what the learner already knows [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].

On the ground (explanation phase): state the objective and the completion standard, cover the aerodynamics and the sensations, the entry speed for today's weight, the procedure, the safety procedures and the exchange of controls, then invite questions [[25:175|AIH 9-5]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

head: Telling-and-doing step
Steep turn application
rows: You fly one left and one right while explaining power, attitude and the sight picture, in the same order you briefed it [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
The learner talks you through a turn: clearing, speed, roll, back pressure and power before 30°, the rollout lead. You hear any misunderstanding before the learner is busy flying [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
The learner flies and says each step aloud. You can tell whether an error comes from a misconception or from motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
The learner flies to standard; you assess against the ACS, then debrief [[25:176|AIH 9-6]] [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

bullets: Demonstrate it exactly the way you want it practiced, including the clearing; learners imitate you. If your demo strays from your explanation, say so at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
Primacy: make the learner's first steep turns correct ones [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
Use simple words. Avoid jargon the learner does not know [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
Integrated instruction: introduce the maneuver with both outside and instrument references from the start [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].
Let the learner practice right after the demo, and allow enough time for it [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].
Debrief: let the learner self-assess first, then compare with your assessment; give concrete suggestions and try not to end on a negative note [[25:176|AIH 9-6]] [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

callout.text: Ground first, then: I tell and do, you tell and I do, you tell and do, you do and I watch.

check.q: In which telling-and-doing step can you best tell whether a learner's error is a misconception or a lack of motor skill?
check.a: Learner tells, learner does: the learner thinks out loud while flying, so you hear the reasoning behind each input [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

chunks.title: Demonstrating from the right seat and keeping control

body.p: On the CFI test you demonstrate and simultaneously explain. Talking and flying to ±100 feet at 50° is a skill of its own: practice the script until the words do not cost you altitude. Explain power settings, attitudes and other factors as you fly [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

There must never be doubt about who is flying. Brief the exchange before flight and use the three steps every time, with a visual check [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. During the learner's practice, guard the controls and be ready to take over, especially on the first attempts at a maneuver [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

bullets: If you need the airplane, take it and calmly say 'I have the flight controls' [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
Anxious learners can be very strong and may react wrongly; there is nothing to gain by fighting a learner for the controls during a recovery [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
Some people freeze under anxiety and cannot act at all [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]. Application: a learner who locks up with full back pressure in a nose-low steep bank is the case to brief and to watch for.
Never let a learner exceed your own limits, and stay within your ability to perceive, decide and react [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
Safety permitting, let the learner go part of the way into a mistake and find the way out; learners who never correct errors never learn to [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

callout.text: Your window for letting an error run is the altitude and the bank. A nose-low steep bank can lose a lot of altitude in a very short time [[24:211|AFH 10-2]], so decide in advance how far you will let it go.

check.q: Your learner freezes in a 60° nose-low bank and will not let go. What do you do?
check.a: Take control and say 'I have the flight controls'; nothing is gained by fighting an anxious learner on the controls [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Then recover: reduce the bank first, then raise the nose [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

chunks.title: Division of attention, distractions and disorientation

body.p: Division of attention between aircraft control and orientation is the point of the maneuver: hold bank, pitch and power, watch the nose and both wings against the horizon, track the heading for the rollout, and keep scanning [[24:210|AFH 10-1]] [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. Throughout a turn the pilot should reference the natural horizon, scan for traffic and occasionally cross-check the instruments [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

bullets: Fixation: a learner may stare at the altimeter while bank and heading drift. Fixation often means the task has had too little practice on its own [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].
How to spot it: glance at the learner's eyes; a gaze stuck on one instrument suggests fixation [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].

Task prioritization: before learners juggle tasks, each task should be done reasonably well on its own [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. Budgeting time and prioritizing tasks gives room to work without error [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].
Situational awareness includes the airplane's position, flight path, other aircraft and the environment [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].

body.p: Distractions are part of the training. Most stall/spin accidents happened when attention was diverted from flying, and the most effective training creates distractions while the learner practices maneuvers [[25:179|AIH 9-9]] [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. AIH examples include reading the outside air temperature, finding a heading on a chart, or identifying a field for a forced landing [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. The CFI ACS also tells the evaluator to use realistic distractions (ACS Appendix 2).

bullets: Loss of situational awareness or disorientation: becoming disoriented is on the AFH error list [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].
Coriolis illusion: an abrupt head movement in a prolonged constant-rate turn can create rotation on another axis; avoid sudden, extreme head movements [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].
If something drops, retrieve it with minimal head movement and be alert for the Coriolis illusion [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].
Graveyard spiral: in a long coordinated turn a pilot may sense wings level while actually descending, and pulling back only tightens the spiral and adds to the altitude loss [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].

callout.text: Do not teach at the wrong moment. The AIH warns against creating a hazard by teaching something at an inappropriate time [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. Application: brief the steep turn on the ground and coach in short words in the air.

check.q: Which distraction from the AIH list would you avoid in the middle of a long steep turn, and why?
check.a: Asking the learner to pick up a dropped pencil or reach into the back seat: a big head movement in a prolonged turn can trigger the Coriolis illusion [[25:180|AIH 9-10]] [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]] [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. Application: use it in straight flight or after the rollout.

body.p: Before any practice maneuver, make sure the area is clear of traffic and other hazards [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. A clearing turn makes sure the next maneuver will not proceed into another aircraft's path. The instructor should teach an effective clearing procedure and insist on its use; clearing plus good scanning is the most effective defense against collision [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

bullets: Scan in eye movements of no more than 10°, each area watched at least 1 second [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].
During instruction, have the pilot verbalize the clearing: 'clear left, right, above, and below' [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].
A target with no relative motion that grows larger is on a collision course; take evasive action [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].
Traffic clusters near VORs and airport surface areas, and most collisions happen in good weather [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].
Practice areas can be crowded, and haze or pollution aggravate the collision hazard [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

body.p: Teach the habit, not just the turn. If learners believe the instructor does all the scanning, they never build the habit; any tendency to start a maneuver without a careful traffic check must be corrected at once. In one study, flight instructors were aboard in 37 percent of midair collisions [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. Tell the learner that you are both responsible for the lookout [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

callout.text: Failure to scan for traffic during the maneuver is a listed steep turn error [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]. Application: in a steep bank the high wing hides part of the sky, and the whole circle takes well under a minute, so keep the learner's eyes outside.

check.q: Why should a learner, not only you, call 'clear left, right, above, and below'?
check.a: Learners who think the instructor handles all scanning do not build the habit of constant vigilance [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]; the PHAK says to have the pilot verbalize the clearing during instruction [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

chunks.title: Uncoordinated flight and low altitude risk

body.p: Uncoordinated flight: the AFH wants pilots to sense a slip or skid without undue reliance on the instruments. In a skid you feel pressed to the outside of the turn, in a slip to the inside; coordinated, straight down into the seat [[24:74|AFH 3-13]].

Why it matters: a cross-control stall happens when the critical angle of attack is exceeded with aileron one way and rudder the other. It can come with little warning, roll the airplane toward inverted and start a spin, and it can be deadly close to the ground [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. The classic case is a skidding base-to-final turn with too much inside rudder, a steepening bank, a dropping nose and a pull on the elevator [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

bullets: Low altitude maneuvering, stall and spin: knowing load factors and VA helps prevent stalls from steep turns or excessive maneuvering near the ground [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].
Controlled flight into terrain (CFIT): mismanaging altitude and airspeed contributes to the three most common types of fatal accidents, including loss of control in flight and CFIT [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].
Low in the pattern, be reluctant to bank more than 30° and never skid around to fix an overshoot; go around [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
In tight terrain, slowing down shrinks the turn more safely than steepening the bank [[1:138|PHAK 5-41]].

body.p: Pick the practice altitude with recovery in mind. The CFI ACS gives no minimum altitude for this Task; the AIH warns against teaching at an inappropriate altitude, such as stalls below a cloud layer that leaves too little room to recover [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. Application: choose an altitude that leaves room for an accelerated stall or a spiral recovery.

callout.text: With a non-crewmember aboard, no intentional maneuver may exceed 60° of bank unless everyone wears an approved parachute. Flight tests for a certificate or rating, and required maneuvers given by a CFI (or an ATP instructing under 61.67), are excepted [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307]].

check.q: In a right steep turn the learner feels pushed toward the outside and the ball is to the left. What is it, and what is the risk if the learner then pulls hard?
check.a: A skid [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]. Pulling toward the critical angle of attack while uncoordinated invites a cross-control stall that can roll toward inverted and start a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

body.p: The AFH lists 13 common errors [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]. Altitude deviations are the primary error, and watching only the nose makes altitude hard to hold [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. For S6 the examiner will fly some of these; name what you see, explain the cause and give the fix.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Insist on a clearing procedure before every maneuver [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]
Inadequate pitch control on entry or rollout
Altitude change as the bank goes in or comes out
Back pressure and power generally before 30°; ease them off during the rollout [[24:211|AFH 10-2]] [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]
Watch nose and both wings; small pitch changes with the bank held constant [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]
Failure to maintain constant bank angle
Ball off center; nose moves before or after the bank
Rudder with aileron; nose first means rudder too soon, bank first means rudder too late [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]
Heavy pull, or forgetting trim on rollout
Trim if used, and remove it as the maneuver ends [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]
Add power as the bank and angle of attack increase [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]
Stabilize at the entry speed, then manage power [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]
Performing by reference to the flight instruments
Eyes inside, fixed on one gauge
Outside references first, quick cross-check; watch the learner's eyes [[24:77|AFH 3-16]] [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]
Failure to scan for other traffic
No head movement during the turn
Scan as part of every circle [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]
Rollout begun well before the lead point
Lead by half the bank: about 25° at 50° [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]
Failure to stop the turn on the designated heading
Lead by half the bank and use the distant reference [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]

body.p: The big one: nose low, steep bank, altitude going fast. Recover by first reducing the bank with coordinated opposite aileron and rudder, then raising the pitch with back pressure. Elevator alone only steepens the bank and stresses the airplane [[24:211|AFH 10-2]] [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

How to analyze: decide whether the error comes from a misconception or from motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. If you suspect the learner flies it right without understanding, have them vary it slightly or combine it with another maneuver [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. If a deficiency needs reteaching, demonstrate again, let the learner practice under direction, then evaluate [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

callout.text: Critique right after the performance while it is fresh, cover good as well as bad, and offer concrete fixes [[25:141|AIH 6-10]] [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

check.q: Learner's turn: nose low, 58° of bank, altitude dropping. What two steps do you coach, in order?
check.a: Reduce the bank with coordinated opposite aileron and rudder, then raise the nose with back pressure [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

f1.caption: Figure 10-1. Steep turns. (AFH 10-1)
f1.alt: A high-wing airplane flies along a straight blue path, then flies two connected steeply banked circles that form a figure eight over green fields, one circle to each side, before leaving on the original path. Shadows of the circles fall on the ground.

f2.caption: Figure 3-15. Overbanking tendency. (AFH 3-14)
f2.alt: A high-wing airplane in a steep left bank. A box at the raised outer wing says it travels a greater distance, with higher speed and more lift. A box at the lowered inner wing says it travels a shorter distance, with lower speed and less lift. A curved arrow shows the bank tending to steepen.

f3.caption: Figure 5-53. Angle of bank changes load factor in level flight. (PHAK 5-34)
f3.alt: A graph of load factor in G units from 0 to 7 against bank angle from 0 to 90 degrees. The curve starts at 1 G, rises slowly to about 1.4 G at 45 degrees and 2 G at 60 degrees, then shoots up steeply, near 4 G a little past 75 degrees, and runs off the top of the chart just past 80 degrees.

f4.caption: Figure 3-13. Indications of a slip and skid. (AFH 3-13)
f4.alt: Three panels: skid, coordinated turn and slip. Each shows an attitude indicator, a turn coordinator and a seated pilot. Skid: ball to the outside of the turn and the pilot pushed toward the outside. Coordinated: ball centered and the pilot pressed straight down. Slip: ball to the inside of the turn and the pilot pushed toward the inside.

f5.caption: Figure 3-18. Parallax view. (AFH 3-16)
f5.alt: Two cockpit views from the left seat. In a left turn the pilot moves lower relative to the roll axis and the natural horizon reference appears higher above the glareshield. In a right turn the pilot moves higher relative to the roll axis and the horizon reference appears lower. Red arrows mark the roll axis and the direction of each turn.

f6.caption: Figure 9-7. Comparison of the teaching process, the demonstration-performance method and the telling-and-doing technique. (AIH 9-7)
f6.alt: A three-column table. Traditional teaching process: preparation, presentation, application, review and evaluation. Demonstration-performance method: explanation, demonstration, learner performance supervision, evaluation. Telling-and-doing technique: preparation; instructor tells, instructor does; a highlighted step, learner tells, instructor does; learner tells, learner does; learner does, instructor evaluates.

f7.caption: Figure 9-8. Positive exchange of flight controls. (AIH 9-9)
f7.alt: Three stacked boxes. One: when the flight instructor wishes the learner to take control, the instructor says 'You have the flight controls.' Two: the learner acknowledges immediately by saying 'I have the flight controls.' Three: the flight instructor again says 'You have the flight controls.' The caption adds that a visual check is recommended and there should never be any doubt about who is flying.

scenario.title: First steep turn lesson with a new private student
scenario.setup: You are a new CFI flying a two-seat trainer with a private pilot student who has just mastered medium-bank turns. The airplane is light today: two people and partial fuel, and the POH shows VA dropping with weight. The practice area is hazy, sits near a VOR, and two other school airplanes are working it. Your student is nervous; the last stall lesson left them tense. Today's plan is the first steep turns.

questions.q: What do you cover on the ground, given the student's nerves?
questions.a: Objective and standard, the aerodynamics, the entry speed for today's weight, and the sensations to expect, treating the fear as normal [[25:45|AIH 2-12]] [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. Brief the exchange of controls too [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

questions.q: What entry speed do you brief, and why not the max-gross VA?
questions.a: The POH steep turn speed, or a speed not above VA for today's weight (ACS AI.IX.A.S2). VA goes down as weight goes down [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]], and above VA the airplane can reach its limit load before it stalls [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

questions.q: How do you handle clearing with the haze, the VOR and the other trainers?
questions.a: Have the student make the clearing turns and call 'clear left, right, above, and below' [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]] [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]. Traffic clusters near VORs [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]] and haze makes the hazard worse [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]; you both keep the lookout.

questions.q: Halfway around, the bank creeps to 57° and the ball sits toward the outside of the turn. What do you tell the student?
questions.a: The overbanking tendency is rolling it in: hold a little opposite aileron [[24:75|AFH 3-14]]. The ball outside the turn shows a skid, so use rudder to center it [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]. 57° is outside ±5° of 50° (ACS AI.IX.A.S5).

questions.q: The student's eyes are locked on the altimeter and the heading sails past the rollout point. What is going on and how do you fix it?
questions.a: Fixation, which you can spot by watching the student's eyes [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]. Flying by instruments instead of outside references is a listed error [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]; coach nose and wings on the horizon with a quick cross-check [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

questions.q: On the way home the student asks why you would never let them do this near the ground. What do you say?
questions.a: Stall speed rises with load factor in a steep bank [[24:211|AFH 10-2]], stalls from steep turns near the ground are among the most serious accidents [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]], and a cross-control stall near the ground can be deadly [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

skills.do: Clear the area before the demonstration and explain the clearing as you do it.
skills.practice: Fly two clearing turns and call 'clear left, right, above, and below' aloud on every practice flight, then have your mock learner do the calls [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]] [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

skills.do: Establish the manufacturer's recommended airspeed; or if one is not available, an airspeed not to exceed maneuvering speed (VA), and explain why that speed, including how weight changes VA.
skills.practice: Before each flight, work out VA or the POH speed for the actual weight and brief it out loud [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]] [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

skills.do: Roll into a coordinated 360° steep turn with approximately a 50° bank while explaining back pressure, power, overbanking and the sight picture.
skills.practice: Learn the 50° picture from the right seat (the AFH explains parallax for a pilot sitting left of the roll axis [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]; application: from the right side it works the other way), and practice the spoken script until it does not cost altitude [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

skills.do: Perform the Task in the opposite direction, explaining what changes.
skills.practice: Always fly left and right pairs and note how the sight picture and rudder needs differ [[24:76|AFH 3-15]] [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

skills.do: Maintain the entry altitude ±100 feet, airspeed ±10 knots, bank ±5°, and roll out on the entry heading ±10° while talking.
skills.practice: Have another pilot call deviations of 30 feet or 3 knots while you narrate; practice the half-bank rollout lead [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].

skills.do: Analyze and correct common errors related to this Task: watch an examiner-flown flawed turn, name the error, explain its cause and give the fix, taking control if safety requires.
skills.practice: Have a fellow CFI applicant fly each AFH error on purpose while you diagnose it aloud and coach the fix [[24:212|AFH 10-3]] [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

quiz.q: Reading the PHAK load factor chart, after about what bank does the load factor start rising at a terrific rate?
options: After about 45° or 50° of bank
Never; it rises at one steady rate at every bank
Only after about 75° to 80° of bank
After about 20° to 30° of bank, in a medium turn
quiz.why: The PHAK says the load factor increases at a terrific rate after a bank has reached 45° or 50°; it is 2 G at 60° and 5.76 G at 80° [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. That is the range your learners fly steep turns in.

quiz.q: At what bank angle does the AFH say an airplane keeps rolling unless opposite aileron is held?
options: About 45° or more
About 20° to 30°
About 20° or less
Only beyond about 60°
quiz.why: Steep turns, about 45° or more, continue rolling unless opposite aileron is held [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

quiz.q: What does the AFH give as the objective of the steep turn?
options: Precise touchdown control, energy management and short-field technique
Stall recognition at altitude, slow flight and maximum performance climbs
Partial panel skills, an instrument scan and recovery from unusual attitudes
Smooth, coordinated control, outside orientation, divided attention and a constant scan
quiz.why: The objective is flight control smoothness and coordination, awareness of the airplane's orientation to outside references, division of attention, and the constant need to scan for hazards and traffic [[24:210|AFH 10-1]].

quiz.q: Throughout a steep turn, how does the AFH want the pilot's attention split?
options: Mostly on the attitude indicator, with a look outside once every full circle
On the natural horizon and traffic, with occasional instrument cross-checks
Mostly on the altimeter and heading indicator, since the ACS grades those
On the nose alone, since it shows both pitch and bank against the horizon
quiz.why: Throughout the turn the pilot should reference the natural horizon, scan for traffic and occasionally cross-check the flight instruments [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]. A pilot who watches only the nose will have difficulty holding altitude [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

quiz.q: Which formula gives turn radius in feet?
options: TAS squared / (11.26 x tan(bank))
1,091 x tan(bank) / TAS
(TAS x 1,091) / (11.26 x tan(bank))
TAS squared / (11.26 x cos(bank))
quiz.why: Radius = V squared / (11.26 x tangent of bank), with true airspeed in knots [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]].

quiz.q: In a steep turn the outside wing makes more lift. What else does it make, and what does the AFH say to do about it?
options: Less drag, giving a slight skid that you correct with aileron
More drag, giving a slight slip that you correct with rudder
More thrust from the propwash, which you correct by easing off power
A nose-up pitch, which you correct by relaxing the back pressure
quiz.why: Because the outboard wing develops more lift, it also produces more drag, which causes a slight slip during steep turns that should be corrected with rudder [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].

quiz.q: Your learner starts a right 50° steep turn on heading 360 and begins the rollout passing 290. Which AFH common error names what she did?
options: Attempting to start recovery prematurely
Ineffective use of trim during the rollout
Inadequate airspeed control during the turn
Performing by reference to the instruments
quiz.why: Lead by half the bank: at 50° begin the rollout about 25° early, near 335 [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]. Starting at 290 is 45° earlier than that, which is 'attempting to start recovery prematurely' on the AFH list of 13 errors [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].

quiz.q: The PHAK gives two reasons load factors matter to pilots. Which pair is it?
options: A higher load factor raises fuel burn and shortens the engine's overhaul time
A pilot can overload the structure, and a higher load factor raises the stall speed
A higher load factor lowers VA and makes the stall horn sound later than normal
A higher load factor lowers the critical AOA and weakens the ailerons in turns
quiz.why: Load factors are important because a pilot can impose a dangerous overload on the structure, and an increased load factor raises the stalling speed and makes stalls possible at seemingly safe speeds [[1:130|PHAK 5-33]].

quiz.q: The AFH lists what a pilot meets when steep turns are first flown. Which item is NOT on that list?
options: Higher G-forces and the overbanking tendency
Substantial pitch control pressures
A lower stall speed as the bank steepens
More power needed to hold altitude at a constant airspeed
quiz.why: The list: higher G-forces, the overbanking tendency, a significant loss of the vertical component of lift, substantial pitch control pressures, and more power to hold altitude at a constant airspeed. Stall speed goes up, not down, as the load factor rises [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

quiz.q: What does the AFH say a pilot will find once the steep bank is reached?
options: Considerable elevator force to stay level
Less power, since the bank adds lift as well as drag
Steady rudder held against the turn to stop the yaw
Almost no control force, since the bank holds itself
quiz.why: After the bank is reached, considerable elevator force is required to hold level flight [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

final_quiz.q: During S6 the examiner, as your learner, flies a left steep turn at 53° of bank, 8 knots slow and 70 feet low, then rolls out 15° past the entry heading. Which item do you call out as outside the standard?
options: The bank
The airspeed
None; all are within tolerance
The rollout heading
final_quiz.why: The standard is entry altitude ±100 feet, airspeed ±10 knots, bank ±5° of about 50°, and rollout on the entry heading ±10° (ACS AI.IX.A.S3, S5). 53°, 8 knots and 70 feet are inside; 15° is not. 'Failure to stop the turn on the designated heading' is an AFH common error [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].

final_quiz.q: Your commercial learner asks why nobody flies a level 75° steep turn in a trainer. Which answer fits the AFH and PHAK?
options: Above 60°, adverse yaw grows too large for the rudder to cancel in a turn
Above 60°, the overbanking tendency reverses and the bank shallows by itself
About 60° is the practical level-turn limit for the average GA airplane; 75° passes 3.8 G
Above 60°, the turn radius grows too large to keep the entry point in sight
final_quiz.why: For a coordinated, constant altitude turn, the approximate maximum bank for the average general aviation airplane is 60° [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. A standard category GA airplane is designed for 3.8 G, and a level turn at 75° exceeds that [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

final_quiz.q: A learner's nose starts moving before the bank as they roll into the turn. What is the cause?
options: Too much back pressure on entry
Rudder applied too late
Rudder applied too soon
Too little power
final_quiz.why: If the nose moves before the bank starts, the rudder is being applied too soon [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

final_quiz.q: Why does the AFH treat altitude and airspeed control as a safety matter, not just neatness, in maneuvers like the steep turn?
options: Altitude and airspeed are the only items graded on any practical test
Mismanaged altitude and airspeed feed LOC-I, CFIT and approach-and-landing accidents
Altitude and airspeed errors mostly cost engine wear and extra fuel
They matter only on instrument flights, where outside cues are lost
final_quiz.why: Mismanagement of mechanical energy (altitude and/or airspeed) contributes to the three most common types of fatal accidents: loss of control in flight, controlled flight into terrain and approach-and-landing accidents [[24:87|AFH 4-1]]. A nose-low steep bank can lose a lot of altitude in a very short time [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

final_quiz.q: At 95 knots TAS your learner's bank sags from 50° to 45°, the bottom of the tolerance. The radius was about 673 feet at 50°. About what is it now?
options: About 560 feet
About 950 feet
About 1,090 feet
About 800 feet
final_quiz.why: R = 95 squared / (11.26 x tan 45°) = 9,025 / 11.26 = about 801 feet [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]]. Less bank at the same speed gives a bigger circle. About 560 feet is the radius at 55°.

final_quiz.q: Why does a 10-knot-faster entry change little in level-turn load factor but a lot in risk if the learner stalls?
options: Faster entries lower the stall speed, so the learner is less likely to stall but feels a little more G in the turn
Load factor depends only on speed, so the faster entry raises the G in the turn, while the load at a stall stays the same
Load factor drops as speed rises, so the faster entry is safer in the turn and also in any stall that follows
Level-turn load factor depends only on bank, but a stall at a higher speed adds load as the square of the speed ratio
final_quiz.why: For a given bank, a level turn gives the same load factor at any speed [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. Stalling at a higher speed adds load equal to the square of the speed ratio [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]; above VA the limit load can come before the stall [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

final_quiz.q: On her first steep turns at about 2 G, your learner says reaching for the throttle felt clumsy and her head felt heavy. What does the AFH say about this?
options: It means the turn is getting near the stall, so she should roll out at once and add power
It is an early sign of hypoxia, which steep turns bring on even at low altitudes
Pilots may have trouble with orientation and movement when first feeling these forces
It shows a skid, since only an uncoordinated turn presses you down into the seat
final_quiz.why: With a load factor of 2.0 the effective weight of the airplane and its occupants doubles, and pilots may have difficulty with orientation and movement when first experiencing these forces [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. Brief it on the ground so it is no surprise.

final_quiz.q: The AFH explains parallax this way: the left-seat pilot sits left of the roll axis, so in a left turn the pilot moves lower and the nose seems to rise. Apply the same geometry to you in the right seat. What do you see in a right turn?
options: You move lower, so the nose seems to descend
You move lower, so the nose seems to rise
You stay on the roll axis, so there is no parallax
You move higher, so the nose seems to descend
final_quiz.why: The AFH ties the illusion to the pilot moving lower (nose seems to rise) or higher (nose seems to descend) relative to the roll axis, and describes the left seat [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]. Application: in a right bank the right side goes down, so a right-seat pilot moves lower and the nose seems to rise, the reverse of the learner's picture.

final_quiz.q: Your learner keeps losing track of the entry heading and rolls out wherever the heading indicator happens to be. What setup does the AFH give that prevents this?
options: Pick distant references before entry to judge when to begin the rollout
Count seconds, since every 360° steep turn takes about one minute
Set the heading bug and fly the whole turn by the instruments
Roll out when the G-load eases, since that marks the full circle
final_quiz.why: Distant references should be chosen to allow the pilot to assess when to begin the rollout [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. Becoming disoriented and performing by reference to the flight instruments rather than visual references are both listed errors [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].

final_quiz.q: Besides overbanking, which effect does the AFH tell pilots to keep in mind in a steep turn because it needs effective rudder and aileron coordination?
options: Ground effect under the low wing as the bank steepens
Gyroscopic precession of the attitude indicator's rotor
Left-turning tendencies such as P-factor
Carburetor icing from the higher power setting
final_quiz.why: Pilots should be mindful of the various left-turning tendencies, such as P-factor, which require effective rudder and aileron coordination [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

final_quiz.q: During an accelerated stall demonstration from a steep turn, the airplane is uncoordinated at the stall. What can you expect?
options: A clean, wings-level break straight ahead
A change in bank until the AOA is reduced
No stall warning of any kind before the break
A stall speed lower than the 1 G stall speed
final_quiz.why: If not coordinated at the stall, the stall behavior may include a change in bank angle until the angle of attack has been reduced [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

final_quiz.q: Your private learner asks whether her examiner will make her fly the steep turn in both directions, as on your CFI test. What is accurate?
options: Yes: every pilot ACS requires a 360° steep turn in each direction
No: the private ACS asks for a single 720° turn in one direction
No: only the CFI ACS adds the opposite direction, for the demonstration
Only if the evaluator specifies; the commercial and CFI ACS always require both directions
final_quiz.why: The private ACS says to perform the Task in the opposite direction as specified by the evaluator (ACS PA.V.A.S4). The commercial and CFI ACS say to perform it in the opposite direction (ACS CA.V.A.S4; AI.IX.A.S4). The AFH describes steep turns as 360° or 720° turns in either or both directions [[24:210|AFH 10-1]].

final_quiz.q: Why is the steep turn taught only after medium-bank turns are solid?
options: Steep turns need an instrument rating, since they are flown partly on instruments
14 CFR 61.87 requires medium-bank turns to be signed off before any steep turn
Performance maneuvers should wait for consistent competency in the fundamentals
Steep turns are a solo-only maneuver, so learners must be ready for solo first
final_quiz.why: Deficiencies in performance maneuvers often come from fundamentals never mastered, so training should not start until the fundamentals are consistent [[24:210|AFH 10-1]].

takeaways: CFI standard: about 50° both ways, ±100 feet, ±10 knots, ±5°, rollout ±10°, while explaining it.
Level-turn load factor depends only on bank: 1.41 at 45°, 2.0 at 60°; stall speed rises with its square root.
Enter at the POH speed or at or below VA for today's weight; VA drops when the airplane is lighter.
Hold opposite aileron against overbanking, keep the ball centered, back pressure and power before 30°.
Nose low and steep: reduce bank first, then raise the nose.
Teach it ground first, then telling-and-doing; brief sensations and the exchange of controls.
Spot errors by watching the airplane and the learner's eyes; fix the cause, not just the number.
cfi_notes: The private ACS asks for approximately 45° and the opposite direction only as specified by the evaluator (ACS PA.V.A.S3, S4); the commercial and CFI ACS ask for approximately 50° both ways (ACS CA.V.A.S3, S4; AI.IX.A.S3, S4). Teach each learner to the standard of the certificate they are working on.

The AIH offers 'drop a pencil' and 'get something from the back seat' as distractions [[25:180|AIH 9-10]], while the PHAK and AIM warn against head movements in prolonged turns because of the Coriolis illusion [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]] [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]. Use those distractions in straight flight, not mid steep turn.

AFH 3-14 says the outer wing's extra drag causes a slight slip corrected with rudder [[24:75|AFH 3-14]], and AFH 3-16 says steep banks need opposite aileron and rudder [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]. The direction is not spelled out the same way in both; teach 'center the ball' and let the airplane show which rudder it needs.

PHAK 5-37 says no combination of maneuver and gust can cause damage below maneuvering speed [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]], but PHAK 5-35 and 5-36 say VA does not protect against multiple or multi-axis full inputs, and alternating inputs can break an airplane at any speed [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]] [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]. Teach the more restrictive wording.

The AFH says certification standards set no trim requirement for steep turns and leave it to the airplane and to instructor and learner preference [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. If your learner trims, make removing trim and power part of every rollout.

Parallax in the AFH is described for a pilot in the left seat, explained by the pilot moving lower or higher relative to the roll axis [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]. No source here describes the right seat; applying the same geometry, your own picture there is reversed, so do not coach the learner from what you see; coach from what the learner should see (application).

Teach the nose-low recovery on the ground first (bank, then pitch) [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]; under stress learners tend to pull first. The AIH lets learners go part of the way into a mistake only when safety permits [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]; decide before the flight how far you will let an error run before you take control (application).

Practice the 'demonstrate and simultaneously explain' script on the ground with a model airplane until the words come without thinking; talking is what usually costs altitude on the CFI test (application).
gaps: Entry speed, VA at each weight, power settings and the published 45° bank stall speed come from the POH/AFM [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]; the PHAK 1.7 x stall speed estimate is only for older airplanes without a published VA [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].
The CFI ACS gives no minimum altitude for steep turns, and the AFH does not either; pick one that leaves room to recover from an accelerated stall or spiral.
No source here tells a CFI how far to let a learner's steep turn error develop before taking control; the AIH only says 'safety permitting' [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].
The sources do not say whether left or right steep turns need more rudder in a given airplane; that is airplane specific.
No source here gives a formula for VA at a lower weight; they only say it decreases and give a 100 versus 90 knot example [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].

activities.title: Read the steep turn picture
activities.intro: Drag each label to its numbered pin on the drawing.

pins.label: Entry: wings level on the entry heading at the entry speed
A 360° turn to the left, the opposite direction
Back on the entry heading: where each rollout should finish
Leaving on the original heading after both turns

activities.title: Shallow, medium or steep?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap the bank class it belongs to.

items.t: Lateral stability slowly levels the wings
Hold a little aileron into the turn
Bank stays put with neutral aileron
Neutralize aileron and rudder once established
Hold opposite aileron to stop the roll
The faster outside wing keeps rolling it in

activities.title: Work the numbers you will brief
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Your learner lets the bank reach 55°, the top of the tolerance. What is the load factor in a level turn? (1 / cos of the bank)
The airplane stalls at 53 knots at 1 G. What is its stall speed in a level 50° turn?
items.why: Load factor 1 / cos 50° = 1.556. Square root = 1.247. 53 x 1.247 = 66.1 knots. Stall speed rises with the square root of load factor [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

items.q: A left steep turn at 50° of bank starts on heading 090. At what heading should the rollout begin?
items.why: Lead by half the bank: 25°. In a left turn the heading decreases toward 090, so start at 090 + 25 = 115 [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].

items.q: How many seconds does a 360° take at 95 knots TAS and 50° of bank?
What is the turn radius at 95 knots TAS and 50° of bank?
A learner enters far too fast and stalls at 115 knots in an airplane with a 50-knot 1 G stall speed. What load factor is imposed?
items.why: Load factor equals the square of the speed increase: (115 / 50) squared = 2.3 x 2.3 = 5.29 G, well past the 3.8 G normal-category limit [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]] [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].

activities.title: True or false: sensations and forces
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: At 60° of bank in a level turn, everyone aboard effectively weighs twice as much.
cards.why: True. A load factor of 2.0 doubles the effective weight of the airplane and occupants [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

cards.s: Control pressure is a reliable index of load factor in any airplane.
cards.why: False. Control leverage varies between airplanes, so control pressure cannot be accepted as an index of load factor [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].

cards.s: In a steep turn a large part of the yaw is felt as motion toward and away from the earth.
cards.why: True, and it can be confusing when first experienced [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

cards.s: A slip and a skid feel clearly different, so seat feel alone is enough.
cards.why: False. Skids, slips and uncoordinated turns can feel similar, a sideways push in the seat [[1:430|PHAK 17-8]].

cards.s: Certification standards require trim to be used in steep turns.
cards.why: False. They do not specify trim requirements; it is airplane and preference dependent [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].

cards.s: Leaning away from the turn to stay upright should be corrected immediately.
cards.why: True. It spoils the use of visual references [[24:76|AFH 3-15]].

activities.title: How a steep turn becomes a nose-low dive
activities.intro: Your learner is established at about 50° of bank. Use the arrows to put the chain in order, first to last, then tap Check.
steps: The learner relaxes the opposite aileron pressure once the bank is set
The overbanking tendency keeps rolling the airplane past 50°
The steeper bank shrinks the vertical component of lift
The nose drops low and altitude falls fast
The learner tries to fix it with elevator back pressure alone
The bank steepens even more and the airplane takes unnecessary stress
activities.why: At steep banks the airplane keeps rolling unless deliberate opposite aileron pressure is held, and a steep bank brings a significant loss of the vertical component of lift [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. It is not uncommon for the nose to get excessively low, losing a lot of altitude in a very short time; recovering with elevator only steepens the bank and puts unnecessary stress on the airplane [[24:211|AFH 10-2]] [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].

activities.title: Match the steep turn error to its fix
activities.intro: Tap what you see from the right seat, then the fix you coach.

pairs.l: Altitude wanders while the learner watches only the nose
pairs.r: Watch the nose and both wings against the horizon

pairs.l: The nose rises or sinks as the bank goes in
pairs.r: Correct the entry back pressure: too much or too little is going in

pairs.l: Large, quick aileron and rudder inputs snap the airplane into the bank
pairs.r: Use smaller inputs for a slower roll and time to correct

pairs.l: Altitude climbs while the bank is coming out
pairs.r: Relax elevator back pressure gradually as the bank decreases

pairs.l: Wings level, but the nose keeps rising with nose-up trim still set
pairs.r: Hold forward pressure and take out the added trim and power

activities.why: Observing only the nose makes altitude hard to hold; watching the nose and the wings against the horizon keeps it within standards, and if trim and power were added they must be removed as the maneuver ends [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. A nose that moves up or down on entry means too much or too little back pressure, and if trim was used, forward pressure may be needed until it is adjusted [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]. Large inputs give rapid roll rates and little time to correct [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]. During the rollout, back pressure, trim and power come off gradually to hold altitude and airspeed [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].

activities.title: Teaching steep turns, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are a CFI with a commercial student in a four-seat trainer, light today with two aboard and half fuel. The practice area is busy and a little hazy.

steps.s: Before the flight, the student says the steep turn speed is the max-gross VA from the POH.
options: Accept it; it gives a bigger margin above the stall
Skip the speed; the ACS only grades altitude
Tell them to use cruise speed
Have the student find the POH speed or VA for today's lighter weight
steps.why: VA goes down as weight goes down [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]; above VA the limit load can come before the stall [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

steps.s: In the practice area the student reaches for the yoke to start the turn right away.
options: Let it go; you have been watching
Clear the area yourself silently
Stop and have the student clear the area and call it aloud
Ask ATC if the area is clear
steps.why: A tendency to enter maneuvers without checking for traffic must be corrected at once [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]; have the pilot verbalize the clearing [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

steps.s: On the student's first left turn, altitude holds but the airspeed decays 12 knots below the entry speed.
options: Coach: add power as the bank and back pressure come in
Coach: lower the nose and accept some altitude loss
Coach: shallow the bank to 30° for the rest of the turn
Say nothing; airspeed is not part of the standard
steps.why: As the AOA increases so does drag, and additional power keeps the airspeed; back pressure and power generally go in before 30° of bank [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]. Airspeed ±10 knots is part of the standard (ACS AI.IX.A.S5), and ineffective use of power is a listed error [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].

steps.s: On the student's right turn the nose drops, bank reaches 60°, and the student pulls hard.
options: Coach: pull harder
Coach: reduce the bank first, then raise the nose
Coach: add right rudder
Coach: cut the power and hold the bank
steps.why: Reduce bank with coordinated opposite aileron and rudder, then increase pitch; elevator alone steepens the bank [[24:211|AFH 10-2]].
